title: (Scenario) An EKS cluster is slow but CPU and memory look NORMAL — how do you troubleshoot across the whole request path rather than one dashboard (Application: latency/error rate/thread & connection pools/downstream DB latency; Kubernetes: pod scheduling/restarts/events/probe failures/pending pods; Node: disk I/O, network, disk pressure, kernel, container runtime; Networking: CoreDNS/DNS latency, service-to-service, NetworkPolicy, LB; Control plane: API-server latency, etcd) — and why are CPU/memory only two of many signals?
shortTitle: (Scenario) An EKS Cluster Is Slow but CPU and Memory Look Normal

s1_definition.profdef: When an EKS cluster is slow but CPU and memory look normal, the bottleneck is on a dimension those two metrics do not capture, so you troubleshoot the whole request path across five layers: the application (latency, error rate, thread and connection pool saturation, downstream database latency), Kubernetes (scheduling delays, restarts, events, probe failures, pending Pods), the node (disk input-output, network throughput, disk pressure, kernel, container runtime), networking (CoreDNS and DNS latency, service-to-service calls, NetworkPolicy, load balancer health), and the control plane (API server latency, etcd health). CPU and memory are only two signals because latency is usually caused by waiting rather than computing, such as a saturated connection pool, slow DNS, or a slow downstream, none of which raise CPU.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India the branch is slow but every teller looks relaxed and the lights are not dimming, so it is not a staffing or power problem. The real delay could be that there is only one phone line to the vault and everyone is queued on it (connection pool), the directory assistance desk is slow to look up extensions (DNS), the central records office in another city is slow to answer (downstream database), or the building's front-gate turnstile is jammed (load balancer). You would never find any of these by only watching how hard the tellers are working, so you walk the entire customer journey end to end.
s1_definition.oneliner: Slow with normal CPU and memory means the system is waiting, not computing, so trace latency across application, Kubernetes, node, networking, and control plane because CPU and memory are only two of many signals.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When an EKS cluster is slow but CPU and memory look normal, the bottleneck is on a dimension those two metrics do not capture, so you troubleshoot the whole request path across five layers: the application (latency, error rate, thread and connection pool saturation, downstream database latency), Kubernetes (scheduling delays, restarts, events, probe failures, pending Pods), the node (disk input-output, network throughput, disk pressure, kernel, container runtime), networking (CoreDNS and DNS latency, service-to-service calls, NetworkPolicy, load balancer health), and the control plane (API server latency, etcd health). CPU and memory are only two signals because latency is usually caused by waiting rather than computing, such as a saturated connection pool, slow DNS, or a slow downstream, none of which raise CPU.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India the branch is slow but every teller looks relaxed and the lights are not dimming, so it is not a staffing or power problem. The real delay could be that there is only one phone line to the vault and everyone is queued on it (connection pool), the directory assistance desk is slow to look up extensions (DNS), the central records office in another city is slow to answer (downstream database), or the building's front-gate turnstile is jammed (load balancer). You would never find any of these by only watching how hard the tellers are working, so you walk the entire customer journey end to end.

**One line to remember:** Slow with normal CPU and memory means the system is waiting, not computing, so trace latency across application, Kubernetes, node, networking, and control plane because CPU and memory are only two of many signals.

sections.s2_technical:
The reason CPU and memory mislead is that most latency comes from blocking on a resource, not from burning cycles. A request thread that is parked waiting for a database connection, a DNS answer, or a downstream response consumes almost no CPU while the user waits seconds. So the first discipline is to stop staring at the two easy dashboards and instead follow the request through every layer.

At the application layer I look at request latency percentiles and error rate, and crucially at pool saturation. A thread pool that is exhausted or a database connection pool like HikariCP that is at its maximum will queue requests, so I check active-versus-max connections and the pool wait time. I also measure downstream database query latency directly, because a slow query plan or a lock contention in the database shows up as app slowness with flat app CPU. Distributed tracing is the best tool here because it attributes the time to the exact hop that is slow.

At the Kubernetes layer I check for scheduling delays and pending Pods, restart counts, and probe failures, because a Pod that keeps failing readiness is quietly removed from the Service and concentrates load on fewer Pods, which raises latency without raising average CPU. Events often reveal evictions or image pull delays. At the node layer I look at disk input-output and disk pressure, network saturation, kernel issues, and the container runtime, because a node with saturated disk or network, or under disk pressure, slows every Pod on it even though CPU and memory read normal. Noisy neighbors and throttling live here.

At the networking layer, DNS is the classic hidden cause: if CoreDNS is overloaded or misconfigured, every outbound call pays a DNS penalty of tens or hundreds of milliseconds, which compounds across microservice hops. I check CoreDNS latency and error rate, service-to-service call latency, whether a NetworkPolicy is forcing retries, and load balancer health and connection limits. At the control plane layer, which in EKS is managed by AWS but still observable, a slow API server or unhealthy etcd makes controllers, scheduling, and any in-cluster client that calls the API slow, so I check API server request latency and throttling. The senior point is that CPU and memory are just two of a dozen signals, and latency debugging is fundamentally about finding where time is spent waiting, which means correlating traces, pool metrics, DNS metrics, node input-output, and control-plane latency rather than trusting a single green dashboard.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India our Transfer Service got slow one afternoon, yet CPU and memory were a calm forty percent, which is exactly the trap this question describes. The scenario reproduces the end-to-end hunt.

Problem 1 — transfers were taking three seconds instead of one hundred milliseconds. CPU was normal, so the instinct to add Pods would have wasted money and fixed nothing. This is exactly why we walk the whole path.

Problem 2 — tracing showed the time was spent waiting on a database connection because HikariCP was saturated at its maximum, and separately CoreDNS latency had spiked, adding a penalty to every downstream call. Neither shows on a CPU graph. Fixing the pool size and the DNS issue restored latency.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `LatencyTracer` that attributes a transfer's total time across the five layers, a `ConnectionPool` that can saturate, and a `DnsResolver` whose latency can spike. It traces a slow transfer for Rajesh and Priya, pinpoints the waiting hops while CPU reads normal, then re-runs after the fixes to show the latency drop.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the latency attribution simulation
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/latency/*.java
java -cp out com.bank.latency.LatencyDemo

# Real EKS: walk the whole path, not one dashboard
kubectl top nodes; kubectl top pods                 # node/pod CPU+mem (necessary, not sufficient)
kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running               # restarts / pending / crashloops
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns      # CoreDNS latency/errors
# App: Prometheus hikaricp_connections_pending, http_server_requests p99
# Node: node_disk_io_time, node_network_* ; Control plane: apiserver_request_duration
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer traced while CPU reads a normal forty percent, first slow and then after fixes.

Step 1 — The slow trace runs with CPU at forty percent, which looks healthy. The connection pool is set to ten active out of ten maximum, so it is saturated, and CoreDNS latency is set to three hundred milliseconds because of a DNS spike.

Step 2 — The tracer attributes the total time across spans: forty milliseconds of application compute, three hundred milliseconds of DNS resolution, two thousand five hundred milliseconds of pool wait because the pool is saturated, and sixty milliseconds of database query. The total is two thousand nine hundred milliseconds, far above the target, while CPU stayed normal.

Step 3 — The tracer identifies the biggest span, the pool wait, as the bottleneck and reports that it is waiting rather than CPU, also flagging the elevated DNS latency. This is exactly the real-world finding: the time is spent blocking, not computing.

Step 4 — We apply the fixes by enlarging the connection pool so it has headroom at twelve active out of thirty, and by fixing CoreDNS so DNS latency drops back to three milliseconds.

Step 5 — The tracer re-runs with the same normal CPU. Now the pool wait is five milliseconds and DNS is three milliseconds, so the total falls to roughly one hundred milliseconds. The transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya completes fast, proving that the fix targeted the real waiting bottleneck rather than adding compute.

```

2026-10-30 01:05:00.103 [INFO]   span pool-wait (app/db) = 2500ms
2026-10-30 01:05:00.104 [INFO]   span db-query (downstream) = 60ms
2026-10-30 01:05:00.105 [WARNING] bottleneck = 'pool-wait (app/db)' (WAIT not CPU) — pool.saturated=true, dns=300ms
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When a cluster is slow but CPU and memory look normal, I immediately stop trusting those two dashboards, because latency is almost always about time spent waiting rather than time spent computing. A request thread parked on a saturated connection pool, a slow DNS lookup, or a slow downstream call consumes almost no CPU while the user waits seconds, so a green CPU graph is expected and tells me nothing about the real problem. CPU and memory are just two signals among a dozen.

So I troubleshoot the whole request path across five layers. At the application layer I look at latency percentiles, error rate, and especially pool saturation, checking active-versus-maximum connections and pool wait time, and I measure downstream database query latency directly, with distributed tracing attributing time to the exact slow hop. At the Kubernetes layer I check for pending Pods, restarts, probe failures, and events, because a Pod failing readiness is quietly pulled from the Service and concentrates load on fewer Pods. At the node layer I check disk input-output, disk pressure, network saturation, and the container runtime, because a saturated or pressured node slows every Pod on it with normal CPU. At the networking layer I treat DNS as a prime suspect, because an overloaded CoreDNS adds a penalty to every outbound call that compounds across microservice hops, and I also check service-to-service latency, NetworkPolicy-induced retries, and load balancer health. At the control plane layer I check API server and etcd latency, because a slow control plane slows scheduling and any in-cluster client.

The reason this breadth matters is that the wrong instinct, adding more Pods because the system is slow, wastes money and fixes nothing when the bottleneck is a connection pool or DNS. In my project at the National Bank of India our Transfer Service suddenly took three seconds instead of a hundred milliseconds while CPU sat at a calm forty percent. Tracing showed the time was spent waiting on a saturated HikariCP pool, and separately CoreDNS latency had spiked and was taxing every downstream call. Neither would ever appear on a CPU graph. Enlarging the connection pool so it had headroom and fixing the CoreDNS issue brought latency back to around a hundred milliseconds. The lesson I carry is that latency debugging is about finding where time is spent waiting, which means correlating traces, pool metrics, DNS metrics, node input-output, and control-plane latency across the entire path rather than concluding everything is fine because two dashboards are green.
